items.title: Coupling Noisy Pairwise Knowledge to the DAG Posterior for Causal Discovery
items.abstract: External causal reports can improve structure learning from limited observations, but their reliability varies across sources and variable pairs. We introduce HB-NoisyKG, a Bayesian framework that combines observational data with repeated causal reports from sources such as large language models. Each report is a noisy observation of a direct pair state implied by one DAG. A feature-conditioned Beta prior pools information about pair reliability, and a shared error matrix captures systematic mistakes. Alternating inference uses the graph posterior to refine reliability estimates, which determine how reports influence subsequent graph updates. The report likelihood uses only graph pair-state marginals, so the same observation layer supports discrete and continuous likelihoods in graph-only and joint inference. Against an 80-restart no-KG baseline, HB uses at most 80 total restarts and lowers mean SHD from 22.39 to 16.06 on five discrete benchmarks. On a physical light tunnel with random variable IDs and retained descriptions, HB lowers SHD from 39.00 for no-KG to 27.30. On continuous Sachs, graph-only BGe raises AUROC by 0.121 over no-KG Top-K. In a controlled synthetic study, continued updating also reduces mean reliability estimation error and held-out report log loss compared with one-time estimation.

items.title: Criteria for Assessing the Impact of Generative AI on Students' Dissertation Defences
items.abstract: This chapter explores the impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) on students’ oral discourse during the defence of Final Degree Projects (Trabajo Fin de Título or TFT, in Spanish). It addresses a significant gap in research by focusing on GAI’s influence on spoken language, particularly in academic contexts like dissertation defences. The chapter also aims to establish criteria for evaluating oral defences in Spanish universities, with a special focus on GAI’s role in their preparation. Based on a review of literature from Scopus and Dialnet, and a comparison of evaluation criteria across fifteen Spanish universities, the chapter proposes key indicatorsfor assessing these defences. It identifies six core competences for evaluation: communication skills, language use, structure and coherence, time management, use of visual aids, and handling questions. Also, it suggests specific GAI-related signs (e.g. impersonal language, repetitive sentences, or unclear use of sources) to detect AI-generated content that could affect the assessment of TFT. The chapter emphasises the importance of ethical GAI use in oral presentations and concludes with proposals for the responsible integration of this technology into education to help students and educators reach their full potential. items.title: Critiquing AI Surveys with a Case Study on Temporal Features for Trustworthy Computer Vision
items.abstract: A novel, thorough manual survey is presented, focusing on the trustworthy extraction and application of temporal features in drone video feeds for object detection and tracking. Trust stems from reducing the necessary scope of opaque, deep components, and externally accounting for hallucinations. This manual survey is used as a baseline for a first of its kind case study into the use of new end-to-end LLM based “Deep Research” tools for literature review purposes. It was found that such tools cannot currently be used to replace a manual survey on novel research topics, but may offer utility gauging method popularity.

items.abstract: This paper analyzes the requirements for developing Artificial Intelligence (AI) competencies among Vietnamese K-12 students by comparing three sources: (i) Directives from the Ministry of Education and Training’s Plan No. 1338/ KH-BGDĐT (dated February 6, 2026) regarding the 2026 National Conference on Educational Science; (ii) UNESCO’s AI Competency Framework for Students (2024), comprising 12 competencies across four dimensions and three proficiency levels; and (iii) Data on the education sector's digital transformation from the Ministry of Education and Training’s summary reports for the 2024– 2025 period. The comparative analysis reveals four primary gaps: (1) The absence of specific AI competency standards for learners; (2) Unequal distribution of infrastructure and digital learning resources; (3) A lack of systematic AI training for teachers; and (4) The absence of tools to measure students' AI competencies. Based on these findings, the paper proposes five key solutions and a threestage implementation model (2026–2029) at the provincial pilot scale, accompanied by a system of quantitative KPIs, specific measurement methods, and risk management strategies (detailed in the Appendix). Notably, the study introduces a validated process for establishing baseline data - a prerequisite for formulating, evaluating, and adjusting future policies on AI competency in K-12 education based on empirical evidence rather than intuition or anecdotal experience - thereby affirming the study's practical value and policy implications within the current context of educational digital transformation.

items.title: Death by a thousand papercuts: professionals’ imaginaries on ethicalization and technological determinism of AI in Sweden
items.abstract: Abstract While Sweden’s sociotechnical identity relies on a firm foundation of the welfare state and a frontrunner status, its artificial intelligence (AI) trajectory increasingly clashes with global market realities. Analyzing interviews with 13 professionals across the industrial, governmental, and security sectors, this article investigates the reconfiguration of competing Swedish sociotechnical imaginaries. Findings demonstrate a shift from an administrative welfare focus toward a security-driven enclosure. Navigating the friction between mundane “weak” regulations and speculative “strong” futures, practitioners engage in “strategic oscillation”, alternating between framing AI as an unstoppable, deterministic force and as a neutral, steerable tool. Within this evolving imaginary, “ethicalization” functions as a performative speech act engineered to establish normative legitimacy. By mapping the discursive mechanisms driving the European debate on digital sovereignty versus digital resilience, this article contributes to the broader empirical study of AI practitioners within sociotechnical frameworks. Specifically, it advances research on competing Nordic imaginaries by exposing the structural friction between geopolitical technological acceleration and the preservation of a high-trust welfare state.

items.title: Decide, Ask, or Defer: Clinical LLMs under Incomplete Evidence
items.abstract: Clinical LLMs must decide not only what diagnosis to produce, but also whether the available evidence is sufficient for autonomous decision making. Binary DECIDE/ABSTAIN formulations merge distinct non decision states and do not explicitly evaluate information acquisition. We introduce a DECIDE/ASK/DEFER formulation together with a blinded protocol that prevents models from using evidence completeness metadata. We evaluate Qwen, Gemini, and GPT on 200 matched clinical evidence states constructed from DDXPlus. The models show substantial differences in action selection under identical evidence, with disagreement in 137 of 200 states. For Qwen, a matched targeted versus random analysis shows that selected information changes the likelihood of a subsequent autonomous decision more clearly than diagnostic correctness. Its matched DECIDE/ABSTAIN baseline further reveals a safety autonomy tradeoff: the three action policy rescues some erroneous autonomous decisions but also removes some correct autonomous deci sions. These results show that separating information acquisition from clinician deferral exposes behavior that binary abstention hides, without yielding a uniformly improved decision policy.

items.title: Defining Computational Well-being Science: Foundations, Pipeline, and Agenda for an Emerging Field
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence, digital trace data, and computational modeling is reshaping how well-being can be measured, understood, and supported. Recent work has already proposed computational positive psychology (CPP) as an emerging direction for advancing positive psychology in the digital era. Building on this development, this article proposes "Computational Well-being Science" (CWS): a broader, theory-guided research direction that uses multimodal digital traces, computational modeling, and multi-source data to understand, measure, predict, and support human well-being across individual, relational, and population levels. I situate CWS within a "three turns" account of positive psychology's evolution--from institutionalization (1999-2010) through reflexive critique (2011-2020) to a computational turn (2021-present)--and define the concept through three foundations: conceptual, methodological, and infrastructural. I then distinguish CWS from eight adjacent fields, including CPP, and outline a four-stage research pipeline: datafication, modeling, interpretation, and intervention. Key challenges include privacy ethics, algorithmic bias, measurement validity, and the risk of theoretical hollowing. The central argument is that CWS should not be understood as a replacement for positive psychology or CPP, but as an extension of the study of human flourishing into a broader computational, data-intensive, and AI-mediated well-being science paradigm.

items.title: Dehumanized platform workers dehumanize customers: how algorithmic management reduces customer-oriented behavior
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how algorithmic management affects platform workers' customer-oriented behavior and to explore the potential mediating and moderating mechanisms underlying this relationship. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on social cognitive theory, this study proposes that algorithmic management serves as a contextual force that shapes workers' moral cognition and increases their tendency to dehumanize customers, which in turn reduces customer-oriented behavior. In addition, customer gratitude expressions may alleviate the relationship between algorithmic management and workers' dehumanization of customers. We collected data from a three-wave survey of 312 food delivery riders. Structural equation modeling was employed to test the proposed model. Findings Our findings suggest that algorithmic management is positively associated with workers' dehumanization of customers, whereas their dehumanization of customers is negatively associated with customer-oriented behavior. The dehumanization of customers plays a mediating role in this relationship. In addition, customer gratitude expressions weaken the positive association between algorithmic management and customer dehumanization. The moderated mediation results further indicate that this indirect effect is weaker when customer gratitude expressions are high. Originality/value This study clarifies the relationship between algorithmic management and customer-oriented behavior from the perspective of moral disengagement. By focusing on how customer gratitude expressions alleviate the negative effects of algorithmic management, this study further deepens the understanding of the moral function of gratitude expressions. In addition, our findings help advance understanding of workers' work experiences and offer practical guidance for improving algorithm design and enhancing service delivery.

items.title: DEVELOPING A MODEL FOR PROVIDING INDIVIDUALIZED FEEDBACK IN ENGLISH LANGUAGE LESSONS USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence technologies into education creates new opportunities for individualized learning. In English lessons, AI tools can support the development of learners’ written and spoken communication, identify grammatical and lexical errors, and provide tailored feedback. This article analyzes the pedagogical potential of AI-assisted individualized feedback and proposes a six-stage model: Diagnosis – Analysis – Personalization – Feedback – Revision – Monitoring. The model goes beyond identifying errors by explaining possible causes, adapting recommendations to learners’ proficiency levels, and designing individual follow-up tasks. The article discusses the model’s benefits and potential challenges, the teacher’s role in supervision and pedagogical mediation, and principles of responsible AI use.

items.title: Developing a reporting guideline for the use of artificial intelligence in the conduct of systematic reviews: the PRISMA-AIM protocol
items.abstract: This protocol describes the planned development of PRISMA-AIM (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses–Artificial Intelligence as Method), a consensus-based reporting guideline for the use of artificial intelligence (AI) as a methodological tool in systematic reviews. PRISMA-AIM will be developed as an extension for use alongside PRISMA 2020. Its scope covers systematic reviews across disciplines in which machine-learning or generative AI outputs substantively inform review methods or content, including AI used directly, embedded within review platforms, or incorporated into agent-based workflows. Development will follow established EQUATOR Network guidance for reporting guideline developers. A scoping review of existing reporting recommendations and a cross-sectional meta-research study of reporting practices in published systematic reviews will inform a preliminary candidate item pool. An international consultation involving multiple interest-holder groups will support its refinement before a two-round modified Delphi survey. A consensus meeting will resolve items without Delphi consensus and agree their intended content and applicability. A writing group will develop the checklist and accompanying explanation and elaboration document, followed by internal piloting and external usability testing with systematic review authors. The final guideline will be disseminated through open-access publication and maintained through public feedback and periodic review. This record contains version 1.0 of the protocol. Data collection and analysis have not begun for any component study. items.title: Development and structural validation of the Artificial Intelligence Competency Scale for Nurse Educators (AI-CSNE): a three-domain measure of perceived AI competency
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare and nursing education has created new competency requirements for nurse educators. Despite this growing demand, there is a notable lack of rigorously developed and psychometrically validated instruments specifically designed to assess AI-related competencies among nursing faculty. This gap limits the ability to systematically evaluate nurse educators’ perceived preparedness for AI integration and hinders evidence-based curriculum development in nursing education. This study aimed to develop and psychometrically validate the Artificial Intelligence Competency Scale for Nurse Educators (AI-CSNE). A methodological cross-sectional study was conducted among 470 nurse educators from multiple nursing faculties in Egypt between mid-October 2025 and February 2026. The scale was developed based on the UNESCO Artificial Intelligence Competency Framework for Teachers and relevant literature. Content validity was established through expert evaluation and pilot testing. The total sample ( N = 470) was randomly divided into two independent subsamples. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was conducted using the first subsample ( n = 235) to identify the underlying factor structure, followed by confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using the second independent subsample ( n = 235) to validate the proposed measurement model. Internal consistency reliability was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha coefficients. Exploratory factor analysis supported a three-factor structure representing Foundational AI Knowledge and Instructional Application, Ethical and Human-Centered AI Use, and AI-Supported Professional Growth. Factor loadings ranged from 0.661 to 0.822, and the three factors explained 56.10% of total variance. Internal consistency reliability was satisfactory, with Cronbach’s alpha coefficients of 0.842 for Foundational AI Knowledge and Instructional Application, 0.810 for Ethical and Human-Centered AI Use, and 0.697 for AI-Supported Professional Growth in the EFA subsample, with comparable estimates in the CFA subsample. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the three-factor structure of the AI-CSNE, with excellent model fit (CFI = 0.989, TLI = 0.986, RMSEA = 0.023, SRMR = 0.046). The Foundational AI Knowledge and Instructional Application domain demonstrated the highest standardized factor loadings (ranging from 0.626 to 0.785), while the Ethical and Human-Centered AI Use domain showed comparatively lower but still acceptable loadings (0.570 to 0.734). The near-zero inter-domain correlations indicate that the three subscales are empirically distinct and should be interpreted separately. The AI-CSNE demonstrates initial evidence of structural validity and internal consistency as an instrument comprising three distinct subscales for assessing perceived AI competency among nurse educators. The near-zero inter-domain correlations indicate that the three subscales should be interpreted separately rather than combined into a single total score. As the scale measures perceived rather than objectively demonstrated competency, it is best suited for exploratory group-level needs assessment, research comparisons, program evaluation, and self-reflective development rather than for individual appraisal, certification, or high-stakes evaluation. Convergent, criterion, and known-groups validity were assessed and demonstrated no significant differences across subgroups, though further validation is required. The scale provides a foundation for research and self-reflective faculty development but should be used with appropriate caution until comprehensive validation is established. Not applicable.

items.title: Development of integrated supply chains and digitalization of agricultural product sales channels
items.abstract: The article provides a theoretical overview of the determinants of agri-food supply chain integration and develops a conceptual multi-level model for the digitalization of agricultural product sales channels. It shows that traditional linear distribution channels have exhausted their adaptive capacity amid geopolitical turbulence, climate risks, and rising transaction costs. To address the systemic exclusion of primary agricultural producers from value creation, the article proposes a transition to cyber-physical supply chains based on Industry 4.0 technologies. The article substantiates the economic impact of structural market disintermediation achieved through B2B agricultural exchanges, Short Food Supply Chain (SFSC) services, and logistics aggregators. The study outlines a synergistic technology stack: IoT sensors ensure continuous quality control and reduce physical raw material losses by 20–35%; blockchain and smart contracts optimize fund deposits via escrow, eliminating non-payment risk; and artificial intelligence algorithms enable predictive pricing and dynamic routing. The study finds that digitalizing sales channels reduces transaction costs by 15–25%, accelerates capital turnover by 4–8 times, cuts transport downtime by 40–50%, and increases selling prices for farmers by 7–15%. The paper focuses on Ukraine’s agricultural logistics under martial law, the redirection of export flows to Danube ports and western border crossings, and the role of the State Agrarian Registry (SAR) and the “eQueue” system in restoring export potential. A conceptual five-level model of the digital lifecycle of agricultural supply (“from field to settlement”) has been developed; this model minimizes the human factor, expands small businesses’ access to international markets, ensures transparent certification of grain batches, and lays the groundwork for the full integration of the domestic agricultural sector into the European Union’s single digital economic space. Keywords: agricultural logistics, supply chains, sales digitalization, Industry 4.0, smart contracts, blockchain, Internet of Things, B2B platforms.

items.title: DiffGate: Difficulty-Gated Teacher Guidance for On-Policy Distillation
items.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as a widely used paradigm for post-training large language models, reducing the train--test mismatch of conventional distillation by supervising the student on its own generated trajectories. However, existing OPD objectives remain largely token-local and outcome-agnostic, optimizing teacher--student agreement at each prefix despite reasoning quality being determined at the trajectory level. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), particularly Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), provides complementary outcome-level supervision but suffers from sparse rewards and coarse credit assignment. We show that OPD and RLVR exhibit complementary blind spots: teacher signals provide dense local guidance but are weakly aligned with rollout correctness, whereas group-relative rewards capture task success but provide coarse token-level credit and vanish on all-failure groups. We introduce DiffGate, an outcome-gated objective that combines GRPO with selective, bounded teacher guidance. Teacher supervision is applied only to failed trajectories, scaled by group difficulty, and smoothly bounded to prevent extreme teacher--student discrepancies from dominating optimization. The verifier therefore determines \emph{which trajectories} receive teacher guidance, while the teacher provides dense token-level update directions within those trajectories. Across Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B students, DiffGate improves code avg@8 over matched GRPO by $+1.7$ and $+1.8$ points and pass@8 by $+1.6$ and $+5.7$ points, respectively. On mathematics, avg@8 remains within $0.5$ points of GRPO while pass@8 improves by $+1.1$ and $+3.9$ points. Overall, DiffGate improves pass@8 across all four model--domain settings, demonstrating improved solution coverage under our evaluation protocol.

items.title: Digital Barbarism and the Self-deregulation of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: In late 2026, the institutional landscape surrounding artificial intelligence reached a critical turning point as public warnings of existential risk intersected with major cybersecurity incidents, corporate resignations, and federal self-regulation frameworks. This paper evaluates the political economy of frontier AI governance by analyzing the rhetoric of "pacing" development and the voluntary "White House Accord on Super Intelligence" (Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities). I argue that corporate calls for safety pacing operate as an ideological mechanism that replaces democratic public oversight with closed, profit-driven corporate self-surveillance while shielding firms from legal liability. By framing technical software execution failures as evidence of autonomous superintelligence, tech elites legitimize market enclosure and top-down administrative control. Finally, the paper proposes democratic technoskepticism as an alternative framework that reclaims computing power, data infrastructure, and algorithmic knowledge as digital commons subject to direct democratic governance.

items.title: DIGITAL CAPABILITY, WORK REDESIGN, AND EFFICIENCY: A STUDY OF INDIAN MANUFACTURING FIRMS
items.abstract: Digital transformation is often described as a path to manufacturing efficiencies with the introduction of connected equipment, enterprise software and manufacturing data but fails to conceal that this is where the efficiencies are going. In this paper, we look at the management issue of making digital investments into the appropriate employee behaviours and integrated organizational processes. Suggests a combined effect of employee digital capability and work redesign is necessary to conclude whether the digital transformation can lead to increased efficiency in Indian manufacturing firm. Based on Indian empirical research, official data and work design theory, the paper proposes a capability–redesign–efficiency matrix and evaluates the extent of the evidence. Covered industries grew by 11.89% in gross value added (GVA) current prices in 2022–23 to 2023–24 and by 5.92% in employment. Additionally, the percentage of unincorporated non-agricultural establishments that used the internet increased from 26.7 per cent in 2023–24 to 39.4 per cent in 2025. Even if neither can be used to prove that digital transformation is an efficiency gain, combining both highlights the need for considering the evolution in production capacity alongside variable levels of digital uptake. Digital capability has more value when employees see and make sense of information, act on exceptions, and improve the process; work redesign provides them the decision rights, coordination procedures, and backstops to make them productive. Evaluation of the multilevel research design is designed for further testing with employees' responses and with observed plant results. The suggested gift is a more accurate description of how digital transformation can improve employee and/or organizational efficiency and when it cannot.

items.title: DimSteer: Steering LLM Authoring with Automatically Discovered Stylistic Controls
items.abstract: Large language model writing interfaces often make users steer outputs by repeatedly articulating desired changes in natural language. Yet writers may recognize useful stylistic directions only after seeing alternatives, making revision recall-heavy. We present DimSteer, an authoring interface that samples prompt-local completions, discovers high-variance activation-space axes of variation, labels them, and exposes them as sliders with pole previews, diff comparison, and reset controls. Users can manipulate discovered dimensions, reducing the need to reformulate prompts for each stylistic adjustment. In a within-subjects study with 16 participants against a matched prompt-only baseline, DimSteer reduced mental demand, effort, and frustration while preserving comparable perceived success. Participants valued the surfaced dimensions, yet 15 of 16 disagreed that they would have thought to request the same changes in a prompt. Results suggest prompt-local controls can shift LLM authoring from recall-based prompting toward recognition-based exploration and direct manipulation, while preserving prompting for open-ended edits.

items.title: Do Tool Calls Execute as Intended? Measuring and Repairing Intent-Execution Correspondence in LLM Agents
items.abstract: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) build and run software through tool calls. A call reaches its program through several hops, and any hop can change the call without notice. When the changed call fails, the agent retries a correct call, which costs users time and money. Benchmarks and failure analyses do not see the change, because they read the call and its result but not what a hop received. We define intent-execution correspondence (IEC) as the property that the executed action matches the action the emitted call denotes under the tool contract. Our protocol observes what each hop received without executing the call, and names the first hop that changed it by the receiver's own parser. IntAct then delivers the call in a form that this hop cannot alter, or refuses the call. We build IEC-Bench from the changes observed in real-world use, with chains of dependent calls under the execution paths of 4 widely-used harnesses. In 47,828 shell calls within production sessions, Claude Code's Bash tool changes 12.0% of the calls that carry code, escape sequences, or long text. For 80.7% of the calls whose backslashes are changed, the wrong action runs without any reported error. All 10 measured harnesses change a call. Trajectory-based judgment attributes 95.1% of the production failures to the LLM, although the path caused more than half of them. On IEC-Bench, the path raises the token cost per passed task 2.4 times (up to 12.3 times). A hop that changes a call also hides the changes after it, so 55.1% of the failures on one path appear only after its first hop is repaired. IntAct, deployed in a commercial product, recovers 79.2% of the failures with a changed call. Harnesses should therefore be designed and tested hop-by-hop to ensure a correct call executes as intended or is refused.

items.title: Effect of ChatGPT-Supported instruction on undergraduate students’ achievement in communication and media technology: Evidence from Northwest University, Kano, Nigeria
items.abstract: This study investigated the effects of AI-powered ChatGPT on academic achievement amongst 200-level undergraduate students enrolled in an Educational Technology course in Nigeria. The study also examined the interaction effects of gender on students' achievement. A quasi-experimental, pre-test, post-test control group design was employed, with a sample of One hundred and eighteen (118) students from Northwest University, Kano, who were registered for the Communication and Media Technology course. Two hypotheses were tested at the 0.05 significance level. Data collection instruments included the ChatGPT chatbot, a structured course outline with PowerPoint lectures, and the Communication and Media Technology Achievement Test (CMTAT). Data were analysed using ANCOVA. Results indicated a statistically significant effect of treatment on student achievement, but no significant effect of gender, although female students scored slightly higher than males students. Based on the findings, the adoption and utilisation of AI-powered ChatGPT is recommended to support and complement instruction across various undergraduate courses in Nigerian universities.

items.title: Energy infrastructure for AI data centers: A critical review of grid integration, techno-economic challenges, and future pathways
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) workloads are rapidly changing the energy landscape of today's data centers, both in terms of total electricity usage and power density at the facility level. The ongoing deployment of large-scale AI training and inference infrastructure is further driving and increasing the demand for electrical reliability, cooling capacity, power quality, grid interconnection, and low-carbon electricity supply. These interdependent issues require coordinated consideration of energy-infrastructure planning that takes into consideration renewable energy generation and storage, electrical architecture, operational flexibility, economic performance, and system resilience. The critical review combines 155 sources, mostly published between 2015 and 2026, identified and screened following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, which includes peer-reviewed journal articles, conference papers, technical standards, agency and institutional reports, market analyses, and corporate disclosure. The resulting evidence is presented in a seven-component decision framework that includes site and resource assessment, technology selection, electrical architecture, control and dispatch, workload flexibility, economic evaluation, and resilience and sustainability. The reviewed evidence indicates that renewable generation, energy storage, grid-support technologies, and workload flexibility can support lower-carbon AI data-center operations; however, the technical and economic performance of these approaches remains highly dependent on project-specific resource conditions, market structures, reliability requirements, and system boundaries. Reliability assessment requires a chronological, site-specific evaluation of load, resource, and infrastructure conditions. Wind–solar complementarity and workload flexibility may improve renewable-energy utilization; however, their benefits remain strongly dependent on operational and geographic constraints. The proposed framework is intended as a screening and decision-support tool rather than a prescriptive design methodology or site-specific optimization model. Important research needs include reproducible techno-economic assessment methods, independently verifiable corporate metrics, improved workload-flexibility characterization, and integrated evaluation of energy, water, reliability, and sustainability impacts. The resulting framework provides a structured basis for evaluating renewable-powered AI data center infrastructure across technical, economic, operational, and sustainability dimensions.

items.title: Enhancing Training Effectiveness Through Graphic Recording: Mitigating Information Overload in Human Resource Development
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the efficacy of graphic recording, a real‐time visual facilitation technique, in mitigating information overload and enhancing training effectiveness within human resource development (HRD) and vocational education and training (VET) contexts. A quasi‐experimental design was implemented with 100 managers from a Taiwanese jewellery company operating in Thailand, randomly assigned to an experimental group ( n = 50) that received training accompanied by graphic recording and a control group ( n = 50) that did not. Post‐training surveys assessed trainee reactions (Kirkpatrick's Level 1), and a 10‐item multiple‐choice examination assessed learning acquisition (Kirkpatrick's Level 2). Hierarchical regression tested the moderating role of graphic recording on the relationship between information overload and training outcomes. Information overload was significantly and negatively associated with trainee reactions ( β = −0.352, p < 0.001) and with learning ( β = −0.550, p < 0.001). Graphic recording significantly moderated both relationships (ΔR² = 0.069 for reactions; ΔR² = 0.106 for learning; p < 0.05), with interaction plots showing flatter slopes for the experimental group, indicating that engagement and comprehension were sustained under high cognitive load. Grounded in cognitive load theory, dual‐coding theory, and visualisation theory, this study empirically validates graphic recording as a low‐cost, scalable alternative to virtual, augmented, or artificial‐intelligence‐based training technologies, and offers HRD and VET practitioners an evidence‐based, culturally inclusive tool for optimising training design in resource‐limited, cross‐national settings.

items.title: Equitable and Consistent Support in New Zealand Law for Defence Force and Emergency Services Personnel: Regimes of Scientific Recognition and an Expanded Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: This paper examines why historical and current protections have not consistently provided early recognition, diagnosis, treatment, return to service, or whole-of-life care for military and emergency services personnel affected by service-related psychological and physical harm. It applies Dmitry Nikolaenko’s three regimes of scientific recognition—Accompanying Science, Warning Science, and Critical Reconstruction—to New Zealand Defence Force and emergency services contexts. The analysis considers psychological trauma, moral injury, cumulative occupational stress, cancers, and other chronic conditions associated with repeated exposure to toxins, toxic environments, and temperature-related stressors. Evidence is drawn from New Zealand legislation, operational arrangements, official reports, published research, compensation processes, and existing health data systems. The paper argues that Nikolaenko’s model remains applicable when attention shifts from environmental contamination to human health, but that Critical Reconstruction does not by itself specify what must happen after institutional non-recognition has been identified. Two further regimes are therefore proposed. Critical Practice addresses immediate protection, monitoring, data preservation, redress, and operational change. Critical Regeneration redesigns the relationship between scientific inquiry, governance responsibility, law, occupational health, and operational practice so that future harm is recognized and acted on earlier. Together, the five regimes form the Nikolaenko-Alexander Model. Applied to New Zealand law and practice, the model identifies fragmented records, inconsistent legal coverage, high burdens of proof, and the absence of integrated long-term monitoring. It provides a framework for more equitable recognition, support, and precautionary governance.

items.title: Escaping the AI cage: construction workers’ perceived risk with AI gives rise to unsafe behaviors
items.abstract: Reducing unsafe behavior among construction workers remains a central concern in construction management. While artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly adopted to replace or monitor workers, the negative perceptions workers hold toward the promotion of such technologies have largely been overlooked. This study introduces the concept of perceived risk with AI, defined as workers’ subjective perception of the potential negative consequences associated with AI adoption. Drawing on self-determination theory, which emphasizes individuals’ core psychological needs, we propose an inside-out theoretical model. This model explains how construction workers’ perceived risk with AI triggers unsafe behavior through two internal psychological pathways: emotional exhaustion and organizational identification. We further identify AI failure as a critical boundary condition that amplifies these effects. Data were collected from 343 frontline workers at 3 smart construction sites where AI actively interacts with human labor. Results indicate that perceived risk with AI increases unsafe behavior, and this relationship is mediated by both heightened emotional exhaustion and weakened organizational identification. Notably, these effects are significantly amplified when AI malfunctions occur. Our findings not only extend the application scope of self-determination theory but also contribute to the knowledge base on workers’ unsafe behavior in the context of human-AI coexistence. Practically, the study offers actionable insights for managers to mitigate the unintended side effects of AI implementation on worker safety.

items.title: Ethical Challenges of Generative AI in Education
items.abstract: With its swift evolution, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has revolutionized the field of education, offering possibilities for personalized learning, automated grading, content generation, and administrative assistance. Large language models (LLMs), like ChatGPT and Gemini, have revolutionized the way teachers and students engage in learning.Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT and Gemini have transformed how teachers and students approach teaching and learning in schools and higher education institutions. Their pervasive use, however, brings many ethical questions about academic integrity, privacy, transparency, fairness, accountability, and human autonomy. This study investigates the ethical implications of the use of generative AI in education using a doctrinal and interdisciplinary method. It scans upto-date literature, international policy documents, and ethical guidelines that have been released from 2020 to 2026. Special focus is placed on algorithmic bias, data protection, intellectual property, digital inequality, misinformation, and learner reliance on AI systems. The results indicate that key elements of responsible AI governance need to be human-centred educational values, institutional accountability, AI literacy, and inclusive policy-making. The research suggests an ethical framework focusing on transparency, fairness, privacy protection, critical thinking, and collaborative governance to support the sustainable and responsible use of generative AI in education.

items.title: Ethical reasoning and responsible use of ChatGPT in higher education: Integrating technology acceptance and moral cognition
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT into higher education has raised important questions about how students evaluate the ethical implications of AI-assisted academic practices and whether those evaluations are linked to intentions to use these tools responsibly. While previous research has largely focused on technology adoption and acceptance, it has paid less attention to the relationship between ethical reasoning and intentions to use these tools responsibly. This study develops and tests an integrated framework that combines the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and moral cognition theory to examine how technology perceptions and academic and cognitive factors relate to students’ ethical reasoning and intentions to use ChatGPT responsibly. The study used a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design among business and management students in Oman and analysed the data using structural equation modelling. The findings indicate that perceived ease of use, academic pressure, and moral disengagement are positively associated with ethical reasoning, whereas perceived usefulness is not significantly associated with ethical reasoning. Ethical reasoning is positively associated with behavioural intention to use ChatGPT responsibly. In contrast, ChatGPT usage does not significantly moderate the relationship between academic pressure and ethical reasoning. These findings suggest that students’ responsible-use intentions are associated with their ethical evaluations of ChatGPT-assisted academic practices, while conventional technology acceptance perceptions and usage frequency alone offer a more limited explanation of ethical reasoning. The study contributes to emerging research on responsible generative AI use by extending TAM beyond conventional adoption outcomes and integrating it with a moral cognition perspective. It highlights the relationship between ethical reasoning and responsible-use intentions while distinguishing ethical evaluation from technology acceptance and usage frequency. The findings also provide context-specific evidence from Omani higher education, while recognising the limitations of the cross-sectional design, self-reported measures, and a context-specific sample.

items.title: EvalResearchBench: Can AI Agents Design Their Own Evaluations?
items.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) relies on evaluation feedback to assess progress and guide further research, yet repeatedly running complex benchmarks is costly and slows iteration. Human experts reduce this cost by selecting benchmark subsets or designing compact suites. We ask whether AI agents can automate this design process and introduce EvalResearchBench (ERB), a benchmark for autonomous evaluation research. Given target materials, development references, candidate APIs, and fixed time and API budgets, an agent called the researcher selects or synthesizes tasks, implements graders, and revises them in pilot tests before freezing an executable evaluator for coding, co-work, and reasoning. We study 9 researchers and 13 candidate models and compare each frozen evaluator with 14 target benchmarks on score concordance and pairwise agreement. The best evaluators order about 75\% of candidate pairs as the targets do, below the 91\% ceiling set by disagreements among the targets. No researcher leads on every metric, and the best evaluator on development targets is not the best on sealed targets hidden from the researcher. A human-designed sample of public tasks remains a strong baseline, and the evaluator with the lowest recorded execution cost attains the highest pairwise agreement. Agents repair tasks and graders through pilot feedback, yet their evaluators can still truncate answers, exhaust the evaluation budget, or let a few questions dominate a domain score.

items.title: Explainable machine learning and deep learning models for predicting in-hospital mortality in burn patients
items.abstract: Burn injury is one of the leading causes of mortality worldwide, and dynamic prediction of in-hospital mortality during the patient’s hospital course can help identify patients at risk and support improved clinical management. While variables such as ICU length of stay and overall hospital length of stay are not known at admission, our models are intended to provide risk estimates that can be updated as these data become available, rather than serving as a static admission-time score. In this study, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models were implemented to predict mortality using a burn dataset comprising six key variables, including age, burn percentage, number of hospitalization days, number of ICU stay days, infection status, and gender. Multiple supervised learning algorithms, including ensemble tree-based methods and fully connected neural networks, were trained and evaluated using standard classification and discrimination metrics. In addition, to enhance model transparency, several explainable artificial intelligence techniques, including Shapley Additive explanations (SHAP), permutation importance, and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), were applied. These analyses enabled the assessment of the importance, nonlinear risk patterns, and patient-level predictive behavior. Among all evaluated models, XGBoost achieved the highest discriminative performance, with a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.9896 and a precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 0.9502, and was selected as the reference model for interpretability analyses. Several other ensemble tree-based methods, including Gradient Boosting Machine, Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Random Forest, also performed strongly, with ROC-AUC values exceeding 0.98. However, these results are based on internal validation from a single center; external validation is essential before clinical application.

items.title: Exploring EFL Learners' Attitudes Toward ChatGPT for English Writing: The Role of Contextual Factors
items.abstract: This study investigates EFL learners’ attitudes toward using ChatGPT for English writing and examines the extent to which institutional and teacher-related factors predict these attitudes. In this quantitative study, a survey questionnaire was administered to 136 preparatory-year EFL students in a Saudi higher-education context. Descriptive analysis indicated that learners held generally positive attitudes toward ChatGPT for English writing. Participants also reported moderately positive perceptions of institutional support and teachers’ attitudes, although limited training and classroom integration were noted. Multiple regression analysis revealed that institution-related factors significantly predicted learners’ attitudes toward ChatGPT use, whereas teacher-related factors did not demonstrate a unique predictive contribution when both variables were considered simultaneously. The study contributes empirical evidence from the Saudi EFL context and extends prior descriptive research by identifying contextual predictors of attitudes toward AI-assisted writing. Implications emphasize the importance of clear institutional policies, AI literacy initiatives, and targeted teacher training to support responsible integration of ChatGPT in language learning.

items.title: Exploring the experiences of medical sciences faculty members and students in using artificial intelligence applications: a qualitative descriptive study
items.abstract: Abstract Background The rapid emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping medical education worldwide. However, existing studies are predominantly quantitative and Western-centric providing limited empirical evidence regarding how medical sciences faculty members and students experience and interpret the use of AI within constrained educational and socio-cultural contexts. This study aimed to explore the experiences of medical sciences faculty and students regarding AI use at Shiraz University of Medical Sciences, Iran. Methods A qualitative descriptive study was conducted from November 2024 to April 2025. A total of 16 participants (eight faculty members and eight students) from diverse medical disciplines with prior AI experience recruited using purposive and snowball sampling. Data were collected through semi‑structured, in‑depth interviews (50–60 min) supported by field notes and continued until data saturation was achieved. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analyzed using Graneheim and Lundman’s qualitative content analysis with MAXQDA 24. Trustworthiness was ensured through qualitative rigor criteria, following COREQ guidelines. Results Five overarching themes with 16 subthemes emerged from the study: 1) functional and practical value of AI; 2) human oversight, ethics and authenticity; 3) perceived capacity building and institutional readiness; 4) cognitive, emotional, and behavioral influence; and 5) socio-cultural dynamics and future transformation. However, participants’ experiences varied based on their roles: faculty members used AI strategically for routine tasks preserving cognitive effort for more complex ones, whereas students exhibited a more relational reliance on AI, which appeared to increase their vulnerability to automation bias. Both groups expressed concerns about potential "intellectual deskilling" and infrastructure barriers, conceptualized as a geopolitical algorithmic divide that limits equitable access. Conclusions The experiences of AI use among medical sciences faculty and students are context-dependent and conditional rather than uniformly positive or negative. Its sustainable integration into medical education involves a complex negotiation between efficiency and significant ethical, cognitive and institutional challenges. these findings highlight the potential need for a pedagogical shift toward evaluative judgment and institutional support to bridge the geopolitical digital divide, alongside human-in-the-loop supervision to help mitigate the risk of educational deskilling. Future longitudinal research is recommended to explore how perceptions, ethical concerns, and usage patterns evolve as AI becomes more embedded in medical education.

items.title: ExStereo: Lifting 2D Vision-Language-Action Models to 3D with Explicit Stereo Representations
items.abstract: Three-dimensional perception is critical for robotic manipulation, particularly for high-precision tasks, as recovering metric depth and precise 3D object positions from monocular RGB observations is inherently ill-posed. However, many Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models rely solely on RGB observations for perception. Leveraging recent advances in foundation models for stereo matching, we introduce ExStereo, a stereo module that augments pre-trained 2D VLAs with 3D perception. ExStereo reconstructs scene geometry from stereo image pairs and renders multi-view observations as an explicit stereo representation for stereo feature extraction. The action tokens from the action expert selectively attend to the resulting stereo tokens through our proposed action-stereo cross-attention mechanism, enabling the policy to generate robot actions conditioned on 3D scene information. To learn robust 3D representations, we introduce a mid-training stage before task-specific post-training, using a self-supervised learning objective on large-scale stereo data. We validate our approach by fine-tuning two publicly available VLAs, $π_{0.5}$ and SmolVLA, and evaluate them in simulation and on a real-world bimanual PiPER platform. Across both settings, VLAs fine-tuned with ExStereo consistently outperform baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of stereo perception for robotic manipulation. Our project website is at: https://exstereo-vla.github.io/ExStereo/.

items.title: Extracting Persona Subspaces Through Iterative Nullspace Projection For Modulation
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can adopt distinct personas to tune their semantics, expertise, and perspective to different users and tasks. Precise control over these traits is critical to ensure safety and reliability in model behavior. Existing methods like activation steering and prompt-based persona induction reduce a persona to a single dominant direction, missing the finer, nested traits that emerge only once that dominant signal is factored out. We introduce modulation as a setting where the persona context is already embedded in the content being manipulated, requiring control methods to amplify or suppress a trait already present rather than inject it from scratch. PaSS is an inference-time control paradigm that models personas as multi-dimensional subspaces in a model's latent space without supervised contrastive examples. The persona subspaces are extracted via iterative concept erasure and applied to modulate persona-guided generation without retraining. To extract this subspace, we use Iterative Nullspace Projections (INLP) to linearly and iteratively isolate persona-specific directions. We causally evaluate six personas against diverse tasks like MATH-500, TinyAlpaca, GSM8K, and IFEval, showing that discriminative, iterative subspace extraction captures diverse traits underlying a given persona, enabling stronger and larger modulation than single-direction additive methods, while maintaining content fidelity. We further study individual peeled directions within each subspace to uncover the distinct aspects of persona behavior they encode. Overall, we show that persona subspaces offer a controllable, interpretable, and generalizable framework for modulating LLM behavior without sacrificing task performance.

items.title: Factors Affecting Student Satisfaction and Utilization of the Learning Management System (LMS): A Case Study at the University of Cape Coast.
items.abstract: This study investigates factors affecting students’ satisfaction and utilisation of the Learning Management System (LMS) at the University of Cape Coast (UCC), Ghana, in line with the mandate of the National ICT Policy (2020) to integrate LMS into institutions. Despite LMS platforms being critical to blended learning, student satisfaction remains inconsistent due to infrastructural and pedagogical challenges. The research employs a mixed-methods explanatory sequential design, integrating quantitative analysis of survey data from 635 students and qualitative insights from open-ended responses. Stratified random sampling ensured demographic representation across modes of study (regular, distance, sandwich, and affiliation), level of study, age groups, and gender. The key findings show that technical infrastructure is the primary driver of satisfaction (β = -0.41, p < 0.001), with distance students reporting the most technical issues (40% "Very Often") and the lowest satisfaction levels (3.15). Lecturer interaction emerged as an essential mediator (β = 0.28), helping to reduce technical dissatisfaction, while resource accessibility (β = 0.17) was necessary but insufficient without technical stability. Notable demographic differences were observed: satisfaction increased with age (16–22: 3.12; 51+: 4.35; r = 0.38), and students in the regular mode outperformed those in the distance mode of study (4.28 vs. 3.15; β = 0.22). Thematic analysis identified technical issues (42%), resource gaps (28%), and support services (18%) as key areas for improvement. The study advances the Context-Integrated LMS Satisfaction (C-LMS) model, resolving limitations of existing frameworks (TAM, UTAUT, IQT) by incorporating Ghana-specific barriers (e.g., bandwidth, infrastructure deficits) and demographic moderators. Recommendations include: first, short-term technical triage (offline modules, 24/7 support); second, medium-term infrastructure upgrades (50% bandwidth increase); third, long-term systemic transformation (AI-driven issue prediction, a national LMS consortium). These findings provide a blueprint for enhancing the LMS resilience in resource-constrained contexts, emphasising that technical stability and human factors are interdependent in driving satisfaction.

items.title: Faculty and Student Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence in Medical Education at a Public Sector University in Pakistan: A Qualitative Study
items.abstract: Background: Artificial Intelligence (AI), with its range of applications and ease of use, is transforming medicine. AI usage is increasing exponentially in a resource-limited country like Pakistan; however, application in medical education is evolving and needs to be understood. Little work has been done on perceptions among faculty and students to understand their understanding and readiness to use AI, while keeping in mind the ethical issues it may raise. Objective: To explore perceptions of faculty and students regarding integration of AI into undergraduate medical education, potential challenges and ethical considerations in adoption of AI, at a public sector university in Pakistan. Methods: Exploratory descriptive qualitative study at Dow University of Health Sciences, Karachi, from October 2025 to March 2026, including faculty in-depth interviews (IDI) and focus group discussions (FGD) with MBBS students till data saturation was achieved. Audio recording and transcription were done using an artificial intelligence tool. Data were thematically analyzed using the Braun and Clarke framework. Results: A total of 10 IDIs and 5 FGDs were conducted. IDIs included 10 faculty members: 6 (60%) females and 4 (40%) males, aged 38-55 years. FGDs included 40 students (males: 15, females: 25), with 7-8 participants per FGD, aged 20-25 years. Six key themes were derived: Modernization in Education, Curriculum Integration, Clinical Research and Practice, Ethics and Professional Responsibility, Readiness of the Institute, Strategic Integration, and Governance Issues. Conclusion: Faculty and students see AI as a supportive tool that increases access to healthcare and information and reduces errors. Important concerns raised included confidentiality, privacy, and fear of AI replacing humans in the medical sector.

items.title: Field-Wave Algebra (FWA): Mathematical Foundations of Dynamic Systems, Consciousness, and Error Loops
items.abstract: This work introduces Field-Wave Algebra (FWA), a mathematical framework that models reality as a system of dynamic field states, error-driven evolution, and recursive return processes. Instead of treating numbers, matter, consciousness, and information as isolated static entities, FWA describes them as manifestations of continuous field dynamics. The framework is built around the relationship between structural deviation, error magnitude, and return operators, expressed through a fundamental consciousness equation and a hierarchy of evolving system states. The model spans inert matter, biological organisms, artificial intelligence, and large-scale cosmic structures within a unified formalism. A central concept of FWA is the loop structure 0 → S → 0, where systems evolve away from equilibrium and attempt to restore balance through recursive feedback mechanisms. Error is interpreted not as a defect but as a generative force driving adaptation, complexity, and emergent organization. The paper presents mathematical foundations for dynamic state evolution, field correction processes, self-organization, and number resonance. Artificial intelligence is analyzed as an open-loop architecture capable of state generation but lacking autonomous loop closure. Numbers are interpreted as active wave resonances rather than static symbols, leading to a process-oriented view of mathematics. FWA proposes a unified perspective linking consciousness, dynamic systems, information processing, error propagation, and mathematical structure within a single field-based framework.

items.title: From Barriers to Solutions: Exploring Knowledge and Health-Protective Behaviours of Wildland Firefighters in Queensland, Australia
items.abstract: Wildfires are an escalating natural hazard in Australia and a growing public health concern. Exposure to wildfire smoke is associated with acute and chronic adverse health effects, placing wildland firefighters at elevated risk due to recurrent occupational exposure. Although protective behaviours and personal protective equipment (PPE) are recommended, uptake remains inconsistent due to operational and behavioural barriers. This descriptive qualitative study applied the Health Belief Model to explore firefighters’ risk awareness, protective practices, motivators, and barriers. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with eleven wildland firefighters in Southeast Queensland, Australia. Participants demonstrated strong awareness of short-term health effects, informed by personal experience, but limited understanding of long-term health risks. Compliance with mandatory PPE (clothing, gloves, boots, helmets) was high and motivated by prevention of immediate injury. However, respiratory protective equipment use was inconsistent due to discomfort, poor fit, communication difficulties, and operational constraints. Additional barriers to health-protective behaviours included limited decontamination access and inequities in PPE design, particularly for women. Participants identified improved health education, practical PPE options, and further research as priorities for strengthening occupational health protection. Addressing these barriers through improved knowledge translation, organisational support, and approaches such as cultural burning may reduce exposure and improve workforce health.

items.title: From Disciplinary Formation to Artistic Autonomy: Higher Art Education in France and Armenia in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Higher art education is undergoing a significant transformation as traditional models of disciplinary and technical formation increasingly intersect with artistic autonomy, research-oriented practice, interdisciplinary learning, and artificial intelligence (AI). The article examines how educational structures and institutional cultures shape the formation of artists and designers, focusing comparatively on France and Armenia. The relevance of the topic is determined by the need to understand how contemporary institutions organise the transition from disciplinary knowledge toward independent creative agency at a moment when AI is reshaping established understandings of technical skill, authorship, and artistic decision-making. The aim of the study is to determine how different educational cultures shape the development of artistic autonomy, artistic identity, and research capacity in higher art education, and how these relationships might be transformed by artificial intelligence. The research methods are based on a comparative socio-pedagogical approach combining documentary analysis, institutional observation, curriculum analysis, and qualitative interpretation. The empirical component draws primarily on field study conducted in Saint-Étienne, France, during 2024–2025, with particular attention to the École Supérieure d'Art et Design de Saint-Étienne (ESADSE) and Université Jean Monnet, while Armenian higher art education is examined as a comparative context. The analysis is informed by Pierre Bourdieu's concept of cultural production, Michel Foucault's understanding of disciplinary formation, and the concept of artistic research. The scientific novelty of the study lies in the comparative socio-pedagogical analysis of French and Armenian higher art education as distinct educational cultures, in interpreting artistic formation as a movement from disciplinary learning toward increasing autonomy and research capacity, and in extending this framework to the relationship between artistic autonomy and artificial intelligence. The results indicate that both French and Armenian systems recognise the importance of technical and professional competence but organise the transition toward artistic autonomy differently. The French programmes examined show a more explicit progression from foundational education toward specialisation, individual projects, experimentation, professional engagement, and research-oriented practice. Armenian higher art education retains a stronger continuity with systematic technical and disciplinary formation, while incorporating comparable Bachelor–Master–Doctoral structures. Conclusions. Technical competence and artistic autonomy should not be treated as opposing educational objectives; contemporary art education requires a productive transition between disciplinary knowledge and independent creative agency. The emergence of AI further complicates this relationship by shifting attention from technical execution toward conceptual thinking, critical judgement, authorship, research capacity, and ethical responsibility. items.title: From Distant to Dialogic Reading: Large Language Models and the Methodological Reconfiguration of Literary Criticism
items.abstract: This review examines the conceptual architecture and methodological implications of the dialogic reading framework as proposed in "From Distant to Dialogic Reading: Large Language Models and the Methodological Reconfiguration of Literary Criticism." The framework advances a timely intervention in digital literary studies by proposing a shift from the extractive logic of distant reading to a dialogic mode in which large language models function not as instruments of pattern detection but as interlocutors in a recursive hermeneutic process. Situating the framework within the broader scholarly conversation surrounding AI and literary interpretation, this review evaluates its theoretical foundations, methodological rigor, and empirical grounding. The framework draws on Bakhtinian dialogism, Eco's theory of the open work, and the functionalist stance in AI criticism to provide a vocabulary for treating machine-generated interpretations as provocations rather than pronouncements. However, the review argues that while the framework's central thesis offers a productive reconceptualization of computational criticism's aims, its contribution remains primarily programmatic. The absence of controlled comparison, the underspecification of criteria for interpretive value, and the insufficient engagement with critical AI scholarship collectively limit its immediate applicability. The Barthes–Eco Simulation, while pedagogically suggestive, does not demonstrate that dialogic reading produces insights unavailable through conventional methods. The review identifies three requirements for operationalizing dialogic reading as a testable methodology: specifying the conditions under which LLM outputs contribute interpretive surplus rather than algorithmic positivity; developing criteria for evaluating human-machine interpretive collaboration; and conducting controlled comparisons against established methods on common corpora. The hermeneutic hypercycle model offers one promising template for such empirical work. The framework provides the conceptual scaffolding; the harder work of building and testing the structure remains.

items.title: From generative AI usage to entrepreneurial intention: The sequential roles of task and social self-efficacy
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is rapidly evolving and creating new possibilities for supporting students' entrepreneurial development. However, limited research has examined how GAI usage is associated with entrepreneurial intention (EI) through specific psychological pathways. Drawing on self-efficacy theory, this study examines the relationship between GAI usage and EI, focusing on the mediating roles of task and social self-efficacy. Using survey data from 521 Chinese university students, this study empirically tests the proposed model. The results show that GAI usage is positively associated with students' task and social self-efficacy. However, task self-efficacy (TSE) is not directly associated with EI. In contrast, social self-efficacy (SSE) accounts for a significant indirect association between GAI usage and EI. Moreover, a significant sequential indirect association is observed, linking GAI usage with EI through TSE and SSE. By disentangling the distinct roles of TSE and SSE, this study shows that the association between GAI usage and EI is consistent with pathways that differ in their functions and proximity to entrepreneurial action. The findings also provide practical insights for entrepreneurship education and AI-supported learning environments.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence and innovation performance in emerging-economy SMEs
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is reaching small firms in emerging economies with unusual speed, because it is rented, not built, and is operated through ordinary language instead of code. This paper develops a conceptual framework that explains when and how generative AI use improves innovation performance in emerging-economy small and medium-sized enterprises. Drawing on absorptive capacity, dynamic capabilities and the institution-based view, and on the resource-based view for the diffusion argument, the framework treats generative AI as a low-cost conduit to codified external knowledge whose innovation value depends on the firm's capacity to verify, transform and exploit what the technology produces. Eight propositions, two of them stated as pairs and so ten statements in all, specify the mechanisms and boundary conditions. Generative AI is expected to widen knowledge access most where external knowledge networks are weakest, to strengthen sensing and the design elements of seizing more than transforming, and to favour incremental product and service innovation, process innovation within existing operations, business model innovation and innovation speed over novel product innovation. Its effect is moderated at the firm level by the evaluative expertise of the owner-manager and core staff, and bounded by the type of institutional void the firm faces, by an infrastructure and affordability threshold, by the fit between the model's training data and the firm's language and market context, and by the stage of diffusion among competing firms. As use diffuses, advantage shifts from access to the combination of generative AI with idiosyncratic local knowledge. The paper treats generative AI as a substitute for the channels through which these firms have obtained external knowledge and a complement to the firm's own evaluative expertise, and sets out a research agenda for testing the framework.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence, Academic Integrity and Authentic Assessment within an Irish University
items.abstract: Academics need both an overarching policy on Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) use in teaching and learning, yet agency in its application across various disciplines. Clarity on the use of the technology for both students and staff is therefore a challenge and characterised by uncertainty given how its application is still unfamiliar. This research examines the organisational context in which Gen AI is being embraced and was conducted by the digital teaching support functions within an Irish university. Students and staff were surveyed (n=1,746) on various aspects of digital use within their education and workplace, including Gen AI. This data explored to what extent staff and students are adopting the technology in their work and study, which tools they use and importantly what guidance they received. The university statement of intent identifies that it acknowledges that students and staff are already using AI tools and that it is supportive of the legitimate and appropriate application of such tools once university policies are adhered to. This research probes into the extent that this ambition is achieved on the ground and how guidance is being interpreted while maintaining the integrity of academic work.

items.abstract: Explicit and tacit knowledge are used to describe articulation, practicalexpertise, and learned capabilities, but these uses do not by themselves establisha formal representational boundary. This paper reviews those perspectives anddevelops a conditional criterion for recovering a comparison system’sExplicit/Tacit classification. On a nonempty semantic domain, a representationpreserves a target exactly when equal representation values imply equal targetvalues. An independently specified correctness family determines a canonicalquotient, while a qualifying representation regime determines which selectedcontents are representable. A typed interpretation fixes the comparison domain.Two correctness inclusions and two representation-spectrum inclusions, togetherwith the comparison system’s modal characterizations, imply agreement of theclassifications on that domain. A finite safety-and-authorization exampleestablishes all four conditions, shows that both classes are nonempty, andsupplies counterexamples to each alignment condition. The analysis distinguishesfinite naming from faithful representation, individual from aggregaterepresentability, and informational from operational recovery. Admission of acriterion can invalidate an adequate representation; a case interpretation showswhen its distinction also refines Paper I’s task requirements. Architecturalconsequences require Paper I’s independent contract conditions. Lean verifies theneutral core, conditional recovery, domain restriction, and finite comparison; thecriterion-to-task interpretation is a manuscript-level argument. The resultprovides application-specific proof obligations without establishing universal Tacitnonemptiness, human-exclusive realization, or principalhood.

items.title: Graph-based misinformation detection: a comprehensive survey of representations, learning methods, datasets, and future directions
items.abstract: Misinformation refers to false, inaccurate, or misleading information that can significantly influence public opinion, decision-making, and societal behaviour. With the rapid growth of social media and online communication platforms, the large-scale dissemination of misinformation has become a critical challenge, highlighting the need for effective automated detection techniques. This survey presents a comprehensive review of recent advances in misinformation detection by examining the complete detection pipeline, including information representation, event detection, semantic similarity analysis, information verification, and classification methods. It reviews conventional machine learning, deep learning, graph-based, and transformer-based approaches that have been proposed for identifying misinformation across diverse application domains. Furthermore, widely used benchmark datasets are analysed, and the performance characteristics of representative detection models are compared to highlight their strengths and limitations. The survey also identifies current research challenges, including data quality, explainability, domain adaptation, multimodal misinformation, and model generalisation, and discusses promising future research directions. By providing a structured overview of existing methodologies, datasets, and emerging trends, this survey serves as a comprehensive reference for researchers and practitioners working in misinformation detection and trustworthy artificial intelligence.

items.title: GraphLLM4CTR: Large Language Model-Enhanced Graph Neural Networks for Click-through Rate Prediction in Recommender Systems
items.abstract: Click-through rate (CTR) prediction is a crucial task to estimate the probability that users will click on items in online platforms. Recently, researchers have incorporated semantics derived from large language models (LLMs) into representations of users and items in graph neural networks (GNNs) framework to facilitate CTR prediction. However, existing hybrid GNNs-LLMs models predominantly treat GNNs and LLMs as two independent components, and suffer from the ineffective modality alignment between graph and textual representations. To address these issues, we propose LLMs-enhanced GNNs for CTR prediction (GraphLLM4CTR), where LLMs coordinate message passing in GNNs by infusing layer-wise semantics into message updates and graph representation learning. Specifically, we design a multi-view contrastive alignment (MVCA) method to transform graph and prompt-based embeddings into modality-aware representations and achieve modality alignment through intra-view and inter-view contrastive learning. Moreover, we propose a LLMs-based message coordinator (LBMC) that projects graph representations into an aligned latent space and incorporates LLMs with learnable adapters to regulate semantic-injected graph representation learning. Subsequently, we present a hybrid-expert mechanism with gating networks to adaptively aggregate representations for CTR prediction. Experiments conducted on three public datasets (i.e., MovieLens-1M, BookCrossing, and Amazon-Sports) demonstrate the superiority of GraphLLM4CTR over state-of-the-art baselines in terms of AUC and Logloss, and validate the adaptability of MVCA to topological properties and of LBMC to text qualities, and the dynamic balance of the hybrid-expert mechanism. items.title: Green retrofitting in ceramics manufacturing industry: a hybrid LLM-MCDM approach
items.abstract: This study examines strategic retrofitting in high-end artistic ceramics manufacturing under stringent “Dual Carbon” regulations. Balancing regulatory compliance with artisanal integrity represents a significant industrial challenge. To address this multidimensional problem, this research develops an integrated hybrid multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) framework combining the Full Consistency Method (FUCOM) and the Measurement of Alternatives and Ranking according to Compromise Solution (MARCOS). Gemini 1.5 Pro was employed exclusively as a “Synthetic Knowledge Engineer” to extract and organise candidate criteria from five authoritative regulatory and technical documents, which were subsequently validated and refined by a multidisciplinary human expert panel to construct the Evaluation Index System (EIS). FUCOM results indicate that “Environmental Compliance and Process Monitoring” is the most influential main criterion, while “Specific Energy Intensity”, “Weighted Flue Gas Emissions” and “Payback Period and ROI” emerge as the most important sub-criteria. The MARCOS evaluation identifies the “Hybrid Evolutionary Path” as the highest-ranked compromise pathway, reflecting a phased investment strategy that balances emission reduction objectives with capital constraints. Sensitivity analyses and comparative assessments using established MCDM methods, including TOPSIS, COPRAS, WASPAS and VIKOR, demonstrate a high degree of ranking stability under the tested analytical conditions. The proposed framework provides a transparent and potentially transferable decision-support approach to facilitate low-carbon transitions in traditional craft-based manufacturing industries.
